sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is the Mw 6.3, 2009 earthquake a characteristic event?
2) Are the larger displacement events highlighted by paleoseismological studies along the Paganica Fault the evidence of larger magnitude paleo-earthquakes? Does this imply a non-characteristic behavior of the Paganica Source?
3) How to reconcile the paleoseismological evidence with the long-term morphotectonic signature of the 2009 earthquake source?
4) Which are the sources of the 1461 and 1762 earthquakes? Are the 1461 and 1762 earthquakes ancestors of the 2009 event? Or alternatively, may one of the two have been generated by another sources located along the same portion of the L'Aquila basin? Or by a nearby, adjoining source?
5) Which is the relationship between the deep seismogenic source and the surficial Paganica Fault? Which are the relationships with the other antithetic surface faults bounding the L'Aquila basin?
6) What is the role of pre-existing structures (e.g. compressional faults) in controlling the geometry of the 2009 seismogenic source?

pictures.t: Map of the 2009 earthquake coseismic ground deformation by EmerGeo Working Group (2009)
pictures.c: Map of the field observations of coseismic ground ruptures (from EMERGEO Working Group [2009]). Note that tectonic ruptures were identified along the Paganica Fault, where they were interpreted as due to primary surface faulting, and along a set of synthetic and antithetic faults bordering the L'Aquila Basin.

pictures.t: View of Paganica and Bazzano Faults
pictures.c: View of the basin located beween the SW-dipping Paganica Fault (left) and the antithetic NE-dipping Bazzano Fault (from EMERGEO Working Group [2009]). Both faults showed evidence of reactivation during the 6 April 2009 earthquake.

pictures.t: Detail of the Paganica surface ruptures
pictures.c: Airphoto of the SW-dipping Paganica Fault showing in detail sites where coseismic ground fractures were mapped (from EMERGEO Working Group [2009]).

pictures.t: Map of GPS and DInSAR surface deformation and active faults
pictures.c: GPS and DInSAR registered ground deformation compared with the surface active fault pattern (from EMERGEO Working Group [2009]). Note that most of the faults located within the area that experienced maximum subsidence were coseismically reactivated during the 6 April 2009 earthquake.

pictures.t: Central Apennines seismotectonic map
pictures.c: Map showing the 2009 earthquake epicentral area in the seismotectonic framework of the Central Apennines (from Falcucci et al. [2009]).

pictures.t: Paganica fault trace in the literature
pictures.c: Maps of the surface trace of the Paganica Fault as reported in the literature (from Falcucci et al. [2009]). Note that in hypothesis B the Paganica Fault is connected to the NW with the Monte Stabiata Fault, while in hypothesis C is linked with the Monte Pettino Fault.

pictures.t: Map of the 2009 earthquake coseismic ground deformation by Falcucci et al. (2009)
pictures.c: Map of the Paganica Fault and evidence of coseismic ground deformation (from Falcucci et al. [2009]).

pictures.t: Map and cross-sections of relocated earthquakes of the 2009 sequence
pictures.c: Relocated events of the 2009 earthquake sequence, the cross-sections show the geometry at depth of the seismogenic source (pannel b) and its position respect to nearby sources (panel c) (from Chiarabba et al. [2009]). Note the cutoff of the seismicity at 2-3 km of depth (Sez-2, panel b) and its projection towards the Paganica Fault surface trace.

pictures.t: Map of the relocated 2009 earthquake sequence
pictures.c: Map of relocated events of the 2009 earthquake sequence and traces of Quaternary normal faults (from Chiarabba et al. [2009]). The Mw 5.4, 9 April 2009 aftershock and the related sequence activated a structure located to the NNE, with a right en-echelon step respect to the Mw 6.3 earthquake seismogenic source.

pictures.t: Directivity of the 6 April 2009 main shock
pictures.c: Lower values of Ml computed at stations located SE of the 6 April 2009 earthquake epicenter constrain the south-eastward rupture directivity (from Pino and Di Luccio [2009]).

pictures.t: Slip distribution of the 6 April 2009 main shock
pictures.c: Along strike slip distribution shows two maxima with about 1 m of maximum displacement (from Pino and Di Luccio [2009]).

pictures.t: Map of RCMT solutions of the 2009 earthquake sequence
pictures.c: Focal mechanisms of the 2009 seismic sequence constraining seismogenic source geometry and T and P axes orientation (from Pondrelli et al., [2010]).

pictures.t: Maximum intensities map of the 6 April 2009 main shock
pictures.c: Map of the macroseismic damages showing a south-eastward elongation of the maximum intensities in agreement with rupture directivity (from Tertulliani et al. [2009]).

pictures.t: Differential interferograms of the 6 April 2009 main shock (from Atzori et al. [2009])
pictures.c: Differential interferograms showing extent of the area in relative subsidence and uplift (from Atzori et al. [2009]). Note the maximum subsidence located between L'Aquila and Fossa about 3 km SW of the emergence of the Paganica Fault.

pictures.t: Slip distribution and source model of the 6 April 2009 main shock (from Atzori et al. [2009])
pictures.c: Variable slip distribution constrained by joint inversion of DInSAR and GPS data (from Atzori et al. [2009]). Note that according to this model the maximum slip of about 1 m was at depth, while only few centimeters of slip propagated upward to the surface.

pictures.t: Source model and slip distribution of the 6 April 2009 main shock (from Walters et al. [2009])
pictures.c: Fault model and variable slip distribution of the seismogenic source of the 6 April 2009 earthquake from inversion of SAR and GPS data (from Walters et al. [2009]). Note that the modeled fault is longer than the outcrop exposure of the Paganica Fault and is in overlap with the Monte Stabiata Fault.

pictures.c: Differential interferograms showing extent of the area in relative subsidence and uplift (from Walters et al. [2009]).
